hook: Your car insurance deductible could be costing you money every single year.

blocks.narration: Your car insurance deductible could be costing you money every single year. Here is the ten-second break-even math to check it.
blocks.visual: A miniature clay car parked in a tiny driveway, a price tag dangling from its mirror

blocks.narration: Your deductible is what you pay out of pocket on a claim before insurance pays the rest of the repair.
blocks.visual: A clay wrench and a small coin pile sit beside a dented bumper

blocks.narration: Choosing a higher deductible, like one thousand dollars instead of five hundred, usually lowers your premium for collision and comprehensive.
blocks.visual: Two small dials, one turning up while a price tag shrinks

blocks.narration: Here is the break-even test. Divide the extra risk you take on by how much you save each year.
blocks.visual: A clay calculator sits on the dashboard, glowing as buttons press themselves

blocks.narration: Say one thousand saves you two hundred a year. The extra five hundred of risk pays off after two and a half claim-free years.
blocks.visual: A calendar flips two and a half pages while coins steadily stack up

blocks.narration: If you rarely file claims, a higher deductible often wins over time. And the savings repeat every single year.
blocks.visual: A long sunny road with the car driving smoothly, coins collecting behind it

blocks.narration: The catch: you need that deductible amount sitting in savings. If a surprise repair would put you in debt, stay lower.
blocks.visual: A small glass emergency jar on a shelf with exactly enough coins inside

blocks.narration: Run these numbers with your own insurance quote. Then follow for the next one: what renters insurance actually covers.
blocks.visual: The car drives into a warm sunset as the camera pulls back

captions.hook_line: A higher deductible can lower your car insurance. Here's the break-even math 🚗
captions.body: Raising your collision and comprehensive deductible usually lowers your premium. Divide the extra out-of-pocket risk by the yearly savings to find how many claim-free years it takes to come out ahead, and keep that amount in savings.
